title: Violent Crackdown in Northwest Pakistan Aims to Neutralize Party of Imran Khan
author: Mehr Sher
content:

officers detain a protester following a protest call by supporters of jailed
former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf
(PTI), a day after Pakistan imposed a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
province and suspended the provincial government led by Khan's party, in
Peshawar, Pakistan, October 12, 2026. REUTERS

Two days after the imposition of emergency rule in Pakistan's northwestern
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on October 11, Irfanullah, 27, and his three
brothers joined hundreds of protesters in the town of Bara. The rally was one
of a series of protests against the imposition of emergency rule and the
removal of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's elected government, which was led by Pakistan
Tehreek-e-Insaf, or PTI, the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan.

More than a dozen people were injured and at least one person, a 13-year-old
boy, was killed after police fired on the protesters October 13, according to
witnesses interviewed by Drop Site, images, videos, and hospital records. Four
police officers were injured and 50 people were arrested, [according to
Dawn](https://www.dawn.com/news/2036943). The political confrontation has
brought protests, arrests of party leaders and workers, and communications
disruptions across the province.

"It was a peaceful protest," said Irfanullah, whose younger brother, Munir,
19, was shot in the left foot, according to hospital records obtained by Drop
Site News. "The Khyber police fired at the protesters, and as a result, my
brother and many others were injured." Irfanullah, who like his brothers is a
PTI party worker, remained at Munir's bedside while he was in the hospital.
"We didn't cause any unrest nor did we have any intention of starting chaos,"
Irfanullah said. "We are not planning to abandon PTI. … We are just demanding
and raising our voice for our rights and for peace here, nothing else," he
added.

Habeel Khan, the 13-year-old boy who was killed, worked at an eatery in the
bazaar, and was caught in the gunfire. His uncle told Drop Site that Habeel
was taken to a hospital where he was unable to receive treatment before he was
admitted to another hospital in Peshawar, where doctors operated on him.
Habeel died in the hospital four days after the protest. According to the
hospital death summary, Habeel was shot in the abdomen, sustaining severe
injuries to his intestines and an exit wound in his lower back. His recorded
causes of death included the gunshot wound, cardiac arrest, and septic shock.

"As a child, he worked to earn money only because of his poverty, otherwise at
his age he should've been in school," his uncle said.

undated family photo of Habeel Khan, who was killed by police gunfire in Bara.
Photo used by permission.

Another young boy, whom Drop Site was unable to contact, was selling bread in
the bazaar when he was shot by police. In a video obtained by Drop Site, an
adolescent boy can be seen lying on a hospital stretcher with a gushing,
gunshot wound to his thigh. He says he was shot by local police, adding, "They
are terrorists, they are oppressors."

Many locals interviewed by Drop Site said injured protesters were unable to
seek treatment at local health care facilities in Bara for fear of arrest, or
were turned away because health care providers feared police raids. According
to Irfanullah, Munir initially stayed home. On the two occasions he sought
treatment at a local hospital, staff turned him away because they feared
police would come to arrest him. He later received treatment for his gunshot
wound at a hospital in Peshawar.

Maheen Pracha, the spokesperson for the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan,
an independent watchdog, said it has received reports of police raids in
Peshawar, Swat and Khyber, the dispersal of smaller gatherings, as well as
curfews and military deployments.

"Whether it's the PTI in power now or somebody else, the same laws being made
now will come back to haunt the next government in power," Pracha said.

Drop Site sent a list of questions to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Police but did not
receive a response before publication. The Embassy of Pakistan did not respond
to a request for comment.

According to two "first information reports," or FIRs, filed during the
multiday protests, police allege that protesters attacked and injured police
officers, held some officers hostage, and destroyed government property. One
of the police documents, filed on October 12, calls for the arrest of local
PTI leaders and approximately 85 unnamed individuals, describing alleged
participants as "agitated and extremist workers of PTI" who were armed with
"slingshots, wooden sticks, stones and firearms" and "attacked the police and
fired upon them with the firearms and the intention to kill."

A second FIR, filed on October 13, names PTI leaders and other local residents
and alleges that a "mob" of approximately 300 PTI workers chanted provocative
anti-state slogans and speeches, incited arson, set up roadblocks targeting
government property, held police personnel hostage, and subjected them to
violence. The FIR states that police responded with a baton charge and aerial
firing to disperse the crowd.

PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan and his legal team are challenging the move in the
Peshawar High Court, arguing that the imposition of emergency rule and the
removal of the provincial government violate constitutional requirements.

## Federal Takeover

The violence in Bara unfolded amid a broader confrontation between the federal
government and PTI, which had governed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for the last 13
years. The arrest of former Prime Minister Imran Khan in May 2023 sparked
protests that escalated into attacks on government buildings and military
installations, with thousands of people taken into custody. Khan has been
imprisoned since August 2023 and subjected to periods of solitary confinement,
following a series of cases brought against him after his ouster from power in
April 2022. In recent months,
[reports](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/pakistan-imran-khan-health-crisis-
eye-sons-denied-visas) of Khan's deteriorating health prompted leaders in his
party, his family, supporters, and human rights organizations to call for
improved prison conditions and access to medical care.

The party had been negotiating Khan's access to health care and his release
from prison with the federal government, but the talks stalled. On October 4,
thousands of PTI supporters began marching from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa toward
Islamabad to press those demands.

In response, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif convened an emergency cabinet
meeting, and on October 11 President Asif Ali Zardari imposed a state of
emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, suspending its elected
government on Sharif's advice and citing a surge in terrorism and political
unrest to justify the decisions. The Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, provincial
PTI president Junaid Akbar, Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, and several
other party leaders were detained. Pakistan's Army was deployed to the
province the same day and will remain there throughout the duration of
emergency rule.

"The government is sort of willing to say [Afridi] is in protective custody,
but isn't willing to produce him before a court, or give any evidence of where
he is. This is the chief executive of a province of 45 million people," said a
senior PTI leader, who was in hiding and spoke to Drop Site on condition of
anonymity for security reasons.

Six days after assuming governor's rule, Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said the
province would extract and sell its mineral resources, and specifically
referred to mineral resources in districts including Lakki Marwat, Tank, and
Bannu. He also called for joint ventures with domestic and foreign companies
to develop its oil and gas reserves. The province is rich in natural
resources, including natural gas, copper, chromite, lead, emeralds, marble,
limestone, and coal, and produces up to 50% of Pakistan's total daily domestic
crude oil production.

## Constitutional Challenge

PTI leaders and constitutional experts are challenging the legality of the
federal government's imposition of emergency rule. Asad Jamal, a Lahore-based
lawyer and constitutional law expert, said Zardari's proclamation failed to
meet the constitutional standards required to justify the measures. Citing
terrorist incidents alone, he said, was not sufficient.

"I'm not a supporter of PTI," Jamal said. "So it makes me reiterate that the
constitutional provisions are being used in a very dishonest manner against
one province, which violates the autonomy of a province. It is discriminatory
in essence."

Under Article 232 of the constitution, emergency rule can be imposed in
response to a grave emergency involving internal disturbances beyond a
provincial government's power to control. Under governor's rule, permitted
under Article 234, the president can transfer the provincial government's
executive powers to the governor and allow Parliament to exercise the
provincial assembly's powers.

"The proclamation does not reach that threshold," Jamal said. "They are
alleging that the provincial government does not have the political will to
fight terrorism. How do you empirically and objectively measure a government's
political will in order to exercise these powers?"

On October 15, Pakistan's parliament approved the governor's rule for an
initial two-month period. Any continuation requires further parliamentary
approval, and the measure cannot remain in force for more than six months in
total.

Regarding the removal of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's government, Jamal said that
there is "no provision in the constitution" that says "the provincial
government is disbanded" during a state of emergency.

According to the constitution, Jamal said, the provincial government should
only lose certain powers, but the chief minister and the elected government
remain. "The chief minister was picked up … under which constitutional or
legal provision has he been arrested?"

Jamal added that there's no concept of a governing secretariat in the
constitution or in any federal or provincial law.

"Where has this come from?" he asked. "The proclamation has come at a
particular political moment when the provincial government was leading a
protest march, which would enter the capital," Jamal said, "That is what the
federal government was afraid of."

On October 14, PTI's legal team filed a petition in the Peshawar High Court on
behalf of party chairman Gohar Ali Khan challenging the constitutionality of
the emergency and governor's rule.

"They can declare it unconstitutional, roll back everything done in the past
15 days or so," Jamal said.

Sameer Khosa is representing Gohar in the case. He told Drop Site that PTI
wants the government to disclose the evidence it relied on to justify the
proclamation, including the governor's report.

"One of the things that we are asking for in court is that the material relied
upon by the president to issue the proclamation has to be brought before the
court so that it can be reviewed as to what is the evidence on the basis of
which the proclamation has been issued," Khosa told Drop Site.

## High Stakes for Democracy

The consequences of the federal takeover extend beyond Khyber Pakhtunkhwa,
raising broader concerns about human rights, civilian authority, and democracy
across Pakistan.

The state of emergency and governor's rule is a significant escalation in
Pakistan's longstanding struggle between civilian authority and the military,
according to Aqil Shah, a political scientist at Georgetown University and
author of "The Army and Democracy: Military Politics in Pakistan _._ "

"It's an important setback because the PTI has been … disempowered and
dismantled, pretty much at all levels," Shah said.

The move has not only stripped the PTI from power but has deprived the people
of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa of political representation, leaving them ruled by a
governor and technocrats who effectively act as military proxies, Shah said,
adding that the military's political ambitions extend beyond Munir's personal
grievances, including Khan's removal of Munir as Inter-Services Intelligence
chief. The military's broader objective, he said, is to prevent civilian
leaders from challenging its dominance over national security, internal
security, and electoral politics.

Shah described Khan as "an existential threat" to the military's rule.

"The only political challenge is Imran Khan and the sort of adjunct challenge
of the PTI government KP, and so those have been contained," he added.

The senior PTI leader told Drop Site the party would likely participate in the
next elections, but Shah said the vote was unlikely to be free and fair.

The current federal coalition of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz, or PML-N,
and the Pakistan Peoples Party, or PPP, came to power after an election
[marred](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/suppressed-pakistan-election-report-
imran-khan-pti) by [allegations of
rigging](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/commonwealth-organization-pakistan-
colluded-election-rigging-report-united-nations). Pakistan's election
commission has denied the allegations, but a senior official
[admitted](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/2/17/pakistan-official-admits-
involvement-in-rigging-election-results) to participating in efforts to
manipulate the results.

The military has little incentive to rule directly, Shah said, because it can
exercise power through civilian political allies without assuming direct
responsibility for the country's governance. The country's most popular leader
is imprisoned, while other parties are willing to cooperate with the military,
allowing it to retain de facto power without accepting responsibility for
governing.

Pakistan's 27th Constitutional Amendment, passed last year, granted lifelong
immunity to the president and the army chief, a provision that currently
applies to Field Marshal and Army Chief Asim Munir and other top officers.
Shah said this measure reflects the military's broader interest in shielding
itself from civilian accountability.

"Accountability is always reserved for civilians, and it's punitive and
vindictive accountability," Shah said. "[Munir] wants to be immune from any
sort of accountability for life till he dies. It's not about being in uniform.
It's forever."

_Ali Akhtar Afridi contributed reporting in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa._
